title: Equal souls
hook: caste, gender and race do not measure the soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, wealth: not evil in itself, only in the clinging and the hoarding. Your line was earned and shared. Did a little of what you earned leave your hands for someone else? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

A long strip of cloth runs down the floor of a gurdwara hall. People sit on it in a row, cross-legged, shoulder to shoulder. A banker in a good coat. A student with a backpack at her feet. A man who came in off the street because he was hungry. A grandmother who barely speaks the language of the room. Someone walks down the line with a bucket of dal and fills every plate from the same ladle. Nobody's plate is first because of who they are. That row has a name, pangat, and the floor it sits on is a plain picture of today's idea.
screen: `ONE STRIP OF CLOTH. ONE ROW.` → `THE SAME LADLE FOR EVERY PLATE.` → `PANGAT.`

segments.voice: First, the light. In a hymn in Raag Asa, Guru Nanak says it in a few words. In paraphrase: recognize the Lord's light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. The question a whole society used to sort people, what family were you born into, gets set aside. Not because birth is a secret, but because it measures the wrong thing. Second, a sharp question from a weaver. The Granth keeps the verses of Kabir, a weaver by trade, and in one of them he turns to a man proud of high birth. In paraphrase: if you are so different, why didn't you come into the world by some other way? Everyone arrives the same way. The joke has a point. Third, one human family. In the Akal Ustat, a work Sikhs keep in the Dasam Granth, a line Sikhs quote says, in paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one. Caste, gender, color, nation: none of them is the scale a soul is weighed on. Fourth, the floor again. A teaching like this could stay a nice sentence. The Gurus put it on the floor. Sit in the row. Eat from the same pot. Take the ladle yourself and serve whoever is next, whoever they are. In the langar, equality stops being an idea and becomes dinner. Equal souls is not a claim that everyone is the same. The banker and the hungry man are still different people. It says the light in each is the same light.
screen: `ASA: SEE THE LIGHT, NOT THE CASTE.` · `KABIR: WE ALL ARRIVE THE SAME WAY.` · `ONE HUMAN RACE.` · `PANGAT: THE TEACHING ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `THE SAME LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat one person as an equal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you tend to rank, a little above you or a little below. Maybe a boss, maybe someone who serves you lunch. On the in-breath, see their face. On the out-breath, let the ranking drop, the way a coat drops off a chair. Then think of one ordinary thing you can do today that treats them as an equal: their name used, their eyes met, their opinion asked. The bell holds the time.
Equal souls. The Gurus' teaching that caste, gender and race do not measure the soul; the same light is in everyone, and the langar row puts it into practice. Today's word.
Your line: equal souls. Today, the next time you catch yourself sizing someone up, swap the question: not who are they, but where is the light in them. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara's langar, Sikhs and guests sit together in rows called pangat and are served the same food, whatever their background; anyone may serve.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pangat, the row in which everyone sits together to eat in the langar.

trapdoor: what you thought: equal souls is a modern slogan.
what it means: the Gurus taught that caste, gender and race don't measure the soul; the same light is in all.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's hymn in Raag Asa sets caste aside, and the Granth includes the verses of Kabir, a weaver.

notes: Please confirm Ang 349 for Guru Nanak's line on recognizing the light in all and not asking about caste.
